cc-01-what-is-claude-code.q: Which of these best describes Claude Code?
options: An IDE plugin that autocompletes code as you type.
A CLI agent that reads your repo, runs commands, and edits files with your permission.
A SaaS that hosts your code in the cloud and runs tests there.
A code review bot that comments on GitHub PRs.
cc-01-what-is-claude-code.explanation: Claude Code runs locally on your machine as a CLI. It can read files, run shell commands, and edit code, but every potentially-destructive action is gated by an approval prompt.

cc-01-what-is-claude-code.q: What is the core mental shift of "vibe coding"?
options: Letting the AI ship code with no oversight.
Typing prompts in natural language instead of code.
Operating at the level of outcomes; the agent handles the how.
Replacing your editor with a chat window.
cc-01-what-is-claude-code.explanation: You describe the outcome you want — a feature, a fix, a refactor — and let the agent do the file edits, test runs, and grep work. You still review every change.

cc-02-install-the-cli.q: Which folder becomes Claude Code's working tree?
options: Your home directory, always.
Whichever directory you launched `claude` from.
A sandbox folder Claude creates automatically.
Any folder you give it the absolute path to.
cc-02-install-the-cli.explanation: Claude Code uses your launch directory as the project root. Files outside that root are not visible to it unless you give it explicit access.

cc-03-first-conversation.q: Why did the agent use Read before summarizing?
options: It was required by the system prompt.
It needed the actual file contents to give a grounded answer instead of guessing.
Read is faster than its built-in knowledge.
It always reads README.md before doing anything else.
cc-03-first-conversation.explanation: An agent grounds its answers in real evidence. If it can read the file, it should — guessing from a project name is exactly the failure mode tools were built to prevent.

cc-03-first-conversation.q: What was the loop in this conversation?
options: User → Read → Done.
User → Assistant decision → Tool call → Tool result → Assistant answer.
Assistant → User → Tool → Done.
Tool → User → Assistant → Tool.
cc-03-first-conversation.explanation: Every turn the agent decides whether it needs evidence. If yes, it calls a tool and waits. If no, it answers from context. That cycle repeats until the task is complete.

cc-04-the-agentic-loop.q: Which sequence describes one beat of the agentic loop?
options: Plan, act, observe, adjust.
Read, edit, commit, push.
Prompt, generate, validate, deploy.
Think, write, test, review.
cc-04-the-agentic-loop.explanation: Plan: decide. Act: call a tool. Observe: read result. Adjust: update the plan. Then loop.

cc-04-the-agentic-loop.q: Why is front-loading constraints in your prompt cheaper than adding them later?
options: It uses fewer tokens overall.
Constraints added mid-loop force a re-plan, throwing away work that was done under the wrong assumption.
Late constraints are ignored.
Front-loaded constraints unlock a faster model.
cc-04-the-agentic-loop.explanation: If the agent has already read three files and started editing under one set of rules, a new constraint can invalidate that work. Stating constraints up front avoids the re-plan cost.

options: Everything in package.json restated in prose.
Things the agent cannot figure out from reading the code: hidden conventions, deploy quirks, taste rules you've already corrected once.
A full architecture overview, multiple pages.
Your API keys and secrets.
cc-05-claude-md-and-memory.explanation: CLAUDE.md is for the non-obvious. Anything inferable from the codebase belongs in the codebase. Anything secret never goes in CLAUDE.md.

cc-05-claude-md-and-memory.q: Where does the personal layer live?
options: In every CLAUDE.md, copy-pasted.
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md — loaded on every project, under the project file.
.vscode/settings.json.
It doesn't exist; CLAUDE.md is project-only.
cc-05-claude-md-and-memory.explanation: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is your global layer. Project CLAUDE.md overrides it where they conflict.

cc-06-reading-and-editing.q: Why did the agent re-read the file after editing?
options: To make the conversation longer.
To verify the edit landed correctly before claiming success.
Because Edit doesn't actually write to disk.
It's required by the Edit tool.
cc-06-reading-and-editing.explanation: Trust but verify. The agent confirms its own work with an observation, not a promise.

cc-07-searching-the-codebase.q: When should you use Glob over Grep?
options: When you want to find file *names* matching a pattern, not their contents.
Always — Grep is slower.
When you're searching binary files.
When you don't know what you're looking for.
cc-07-searching-the-codebase.explanation: Glob filters by path/name. Grep reads file contents. Use Glob to locate files; use Grep to find usages.

cc-08-running-tests.q: What's the value of letting the agent run the test *before* writing the implementation?
options: It's faster.
It proves the test actually fails — a passing assertion you didn't see fail is unverified.
It avoids running the test twice.
It saves on tokens.
cc-08-running-tests.explanation: Red, then green. A test that's never seen red doesn't prove anything yet — it might be passing for the wrong reason.

cc-09-git-and-commits.q: Why is `git push` a different category of action than `git commit` for the agent?
options: Push is slower.
Push affects shared state (the remote) and is much harder to undo than a local commit.
Push requires a network connection.
Commit is read-only.
cc-09-git-and-commits.explanation: Local commits are recoverable. Remote pushes can affect teammates and CI; treat them as deliberate human actions.

cc-10-multi-file-refactors.q: What gives multi-file refactors their reliability?
options: The agent's memory.
Grep finds every call site, then a coordinated edit + test run proves nothing was missed.
The agent reads the entire codebase into context.
Static type checking.
cc-10-multi-file-refactors.explanation: Search → edit → verify is the loop. Type checking and tests are the verification step that catches misses.

cc-11-debugging.q: Why is writing a failing test before fixing a bug valuable?
options: It satisfies the test runner.
It proves the cause and prevents regression. A fix without a failing test is unverified.
It's faster than debugging by hand.
It's required by Claude Code.
cc-11-debugging.explanation: If a fix doesn't have a test that fails before it and passes after, you haven't proven the fix addresses the cause.

options: Nothing — they're aliases.
/clear wipes the session entirely; /compact summarizes it to free space without losing continuity.
/clear keeps tools active; /compact disables them.
/compact is faster.
cc-12-slash-commands.explanation: /clear is the nuclear option for fresh context. /compact preserves intent and decisions in a compressed form.

options: Only the conversation history.
A checkpoint of your code, your conversation, or both — captured automatically before each change.
The last git commit.
Deleted files only.
cc-12-slash-commands.explanation: Checkpoints are automatic and separate from git. Use /rewind to unwind an experiment in seconds; keep git for durable history.

cc-13-custom-slash-commands.q: Where do custom slash commands live?
options: In CLAUDE.md.
In .claude/commands/<name>.md inside your repo.
In ~/.bashrc.
Inside the Claude Code binary.
cc-13-custom-slash-commands.explanation: .claude/commands/<name>.md inside your repo is project-scoped. Personal commands can also live in ~/.claude/commands/.

cc-28-agent-skills.q: What's the key difference between a slash command and a skill?
options: Skills are faster.
You invoke a command explicitly; Claude invokes a skill itself when your request matches its description.
Commands can't take arguments.
Skills only work in the API.
cc-28-agent-skills.explanation: Commands are manual triggers. Skills are self-serve expertise — the description line tells Claude when to reach for them.

cc-28-agent-skills.q: Why doesn't carrying 30 skills bloat your context?
options: Skills are compressed.
Progressive disclosure — only each skill's name and description load up front; the full body loads only when a skill fires.
Skills share one context window.
It does bloat context; keep under 5 skills.
cc-28-agent-skills.explanation: The index is cheap; the payload is lazy-loaded. That's what makes a large skill library viable.

cc-14-subagents.q: When is a subagent the right call?
options: Always — fresh context is always better.
When the task is open-ended research and you want the findings, not the intermediate steps, in the main context.
For any task longer than 5 minutes.
Never — they waste tokens.
cc-14-subagents.explanation: Subagents are great when you want a summary of work that would otherwise pollute the main context. They're wasteful for short, stateful tasks.

cc-14-subagents.q: What does a subagent return to the main agent?
options: The full transcript of its work.
A summary it composes itself; the intermediate steps are not visible to the main thread.
Nothing — they're fire and forget.
Tool call traces only.
cc-14-subagents.explanation: The summary is what crosses the boundary. Intermediate work stays in the subagent's own context.

cc-15-plan-mode.q: Why does Plan Mode disallow edits?
options: Edits are slow.
It forces the agent to articulate the full approach before any state changes — so you can correct course before damage is done.
It saves tokens.
Tools don't work in plan mode.
cc-15-plan-mode.explanation: Plan mode is about reversibility. A bad plan caught before any edit is free; the same plan caught after 12 file changes is expensive.

options: In CLAUDE.md.
In .claude/settings.json (project) or ~/.claude/settings.json (user).
In a dedicated `hooks/` folder at the repo root.
Inside slash commands.
cc-16-hooks.explanation: Hooks are configured in settings.json. The project file applies in that repo only; the user file applies globally.

options: It encrypts messages between you and Claude.
It's the standard protocol for plugging external tools into the agent — databases, APIs, SaaS — so they appear as callable tools alongside Read and Bash.
It compresses context.
It's a slash command framework.
cc-17-mcp-servers.explanation: MCP turns external systems into agent-callable tools through a standard protocol. The agent doesn't know or care if a tool is built-in or comes from MCP.

cc-18-spec-tests-code.q: Why are tests written *before* the implementation more valuable than tests written after?
options: They run faster.
They describe the spec, not the code; they force the implementation to satisfy a target rather than rationalize what's there.
There's no difference.
Test-after is faster but less correct.
cc-18-spec-tests-code.explanation: Spec-as-tests is a forcing function. Code-as-tests is documentation of accidents.

cc-19-iterative-refinement.q: Why does sizing tasks small make agentic work more reliable?
options: Agents have a strict turn limit.
Each small step ends in a verifiable artifact; mistakes are isolated and cheap to revert. Big steps compound errors.
Small tasks are faster.
It saves tokens.
cc-19-iterative-refinement.explanation: Small steps create checkpoints. Big steps create one giant diff where errors hide.

cc-20-when-to-interrupt.q: Which is a *good* reason to interrupt mid-loop?
options: You think the next step is wrong.
It's taking longer than you expected.
You realize the goal you stated was wrong, and continuing under the wrong goal will compound the mistake.
You want to add a different feature.
cc-20-when-to-interrupt.explanation: Interruption is for goal changes and destructive actions. Tactical doubts are usually better resolved by letting the loop self-correct.

cc-21-code-review.q: What's a useful framing for self-review with the agent?
options: Ask if the code 'looks good.'
Ask the agent to act like a senior reviewer hostile to churn, and be specific about what to flag (missing tests, unsafe input, leaky abstractions).
Tell it to rewrite the code.
Ask for a summary.
cc-21-code-review.explanation: Vague framings produce vague reviews. The more specific the posture and the targets, the more useful the feedback.

cc-22-pair-programming-flow.q: In an agent-driven pair, what's your role?
options: Type the code while the agent watches.
Articulate intent and review diffs; let the agent type.
Write tests only.
Approve every keystroke.
cc-22-pair-programming-flow.explanation: You're the navigator. The work shifts from typing to articulating and reviewing — that's where the leverage is.

cc-23-nextjs-feature.q: Why does the prompt include both the route, the data shape, and the test in one breath?
options: To minimize turns.
Front-loading constraints (where copy lives, what to test) makes the loop converge in one pass instead of three.
It's required.
The agent can't handle multi-step asks.
cc-23-nextjs-feature.explanation: Each constraint added later costs a re-plan. Stating shape, data, and test up front is one of the cheapest ways to compound speed.

cc-24-tests-first.q: What does seeing all 5 tests fail before any implementation prove?
options: Nothing — it's just a checkpoint.
That the tests are real and exercise behavior that doesn't exist yet — they couldn't have been satisfied accidentally.
That the agent is slow.
That the spec is wrong.
cc-24-tests-first.explanation: Tests that have never been red prove nothing. Watching them go red, then green, is the verification.

cc-25-legacy-migration.q: What's the key constraint that makes leaf-by-leaf migration safe?
options: It's faster.
Existing tests must stay green after every step. The repo is shippable at every commit.
TypeScript is forgiving.
Leaves don't have dependencies.
cc-25-legacy-migration.explanation: Always-green is the invariant. If you ever break it, you're betting on landing the whole migration before anyone else needs the codebase. That bet usually loses.

cc-26-shipping-to-production.q: Why draft the rollback plan *before* deploying instead of after a problem?
options: It's faster.
Under pressure your judgment is worse; pre-written rollback steps are saner than improvised ones.
Rollbacks are easier to plan after.
It's required by SOC 2.
cc-26-shipping-to-production.explanation: The calmest moment is before the deploy. Use it to write the plan you'd want to be holding when things go sideways.

options: A bookmark organizer.
A clone of an existing major product.
A tip splitter for your friend group.
A tiny meeting-notes summarizer.
cc-27-capstone.explanation: Clones don't teach scoping. Tiny real things do. Pick small.
